Female Yellowbelly flounder (Rhombosolea leporina) attain a maximum recorded total length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], a size that is consistent with the larger-bodied members of the Pleuronectidae family. This ultimate length is achieved through a prolonged somatic growth phase that spans much of the species' adult life. The body mass associated with this asymptotic size is considerable, with the ultimate female wet weight documented at approximately 1100 grams [Wwi = approximately 1100 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions reported for New Zealand flatfish populations. In contrast, the length at which puberty is initiated is comparatively modest, with individuals beginning gonadal development at just 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm] in total length. This marked difference between the size at first maturation and the ultimate size reflects a life-history strategy common among iteroparous marine teleosts, where early reproductive activity is traded off against continued somatic investment, allowing females to contribute to recruitment while still approaching their full growth potential over several seasons.

The wet weight at birth for newly emerged yolk-sac larvae is exceptionally low, measuring 0.000478 grams [Wwb = 0.000478 grams], a tiny mass that reflects the species' small pelagic egg diameter of 0.97 mm. This nominal birth mass stands in stark contrast to the wet weight attained by females at the onset of puberty, which is approximately 36.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 36.3 grams]. The difference of over four orders of magnitude between these two values underscores the remarkable growth trajectory that individuals must complete before they are capable of contributing to the next generation. For a female to reach this pubertal mass, she must navigate the planktonic larval phase, undergo metamorphosis with the accompanying migration of the left eye, and settle into a benthic juvenile existence, all while accumulating the somatic tissue necessary to support future gamete production. The growth coefficient governing this transition from the 0.000478 gram larva to the 36.3 gram maturing fish is a key determinant of age at first reproduction in field populations.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to the eclosion of the prolarva from the chorion, is approximately 7.5 days [ab = approximately 7.5 days]. This brief incubation period is typical for small pelagic eggs incubated at warm temperate temperatures and reflects the rapid developmental rate afforded by the elevated metabolic environment. The same thermal regime of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C] is associated with a maximum lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days] under laboratory holding conditions, a longevity of roughly five years that is comparable to other New Zealand flatfishes of similar body size. The contrast between the short developmental time to hatching and the extended adult lifespan highlights the species' dependence on high early mortality being offset by repeated reproductive bouts over a multi-year adult window.

Reproductive output in Yellowbelly flounder has been quantified under optimal thermal conditions. At 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], females produce roughly 3425 eggs per batch [N_R_i = roughly 3425 eggs per batch] and release approximately one batch daily [F_R_i = approximately one batch daily] during the peak spawning period, a combination of batch size and spawning frequency that yields the maximum daily reproductive rate observed in captive broodstock. This high fecundity is characteristic of broadcast spawners that release pelagic eggs into the water column, where per-egg survival probabilities are extremely low. The daily rate reflects the combination of batch size and spawning frequency; individual females may release successive batches over the course of a single season. The energetic investment required to sustain such a high daily output is substantial and likely draws heavily on stored lipid reserves accumulated during the preceding feeding season. This physiological capacity to convert somatic energy into gametes so efficiently underpins the species' demographic resilience in variable marine environments.

The life-history schedule of Yellowbelly flounder is tightly coupled to its thermal environment, with the 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C] regime representing near-optimal conditions for both development and reproduction. The relatively short age at birth of 7.5 days [ab = 7.5 days] ensures that larvae enter the planktonic feeding stage quickly, a critical adaptation in seasonally productive coastal waters at a temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C]. The initial body mass of a newly emerged larva, at approximately 0.000478 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000478 grams], represents a starting point from which individuals must increase their mass by over four orders of magnitude to reach reproductive maturity. Comparative data from related pleuronectid species suggest that this growth trajectory, with puberty occurring at only 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm] and the ultimate total length reaching 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], is shaped by the need to balance early reproduction against the advantages of larger body size for fecundity and competitive dominance on the spawning grounds.
